newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-"SLIM" AND "NONE" ARE CHANCES HOLYFIELD NEEDED.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-"SLIM" AND "NONE" ARE CHANCES HOLYFIELD NEEDED.

text.p: Promoter Don King for once seemed to have it right in the days before the Mike Tyson-Evander Holyfield fight: "Holyfield has two chances to beat Mike Tyson -- slim and none, and none is out of town."
But "Slim" bulked up and "None" returned in a hurry on Saturday night and brought along a bushel-full of audacity and right hands for Holyfield.

Holyfield chipped in his faith in God to carry him through, a faith that at the time seemed unjustified and definitely counter to the bookmakers' bottom line. They had Tyson listed as a 15-1 favourite in the days before Holyfield pulled off one of the biggest upsets in boxing history when he mugged Tyson for his World Boxing Association heavyweight title.
Holyfield's audacity came in the form of first insisting he had no fear whatsoever of Tyson and then daring to show it when, as they say in boxing, he "walked-the talk."
It was the only way to beat him, Holyfield declared with what turned out to be prescience, but at the time seemed closer to pathetic.

Just about everyone else thought they would see harakiri in the ring at the MGM Grand. The conventional wisdom was Holyfield had simply taken too many punches in too many tough fights to survive more than a couple of rounds with Tyson's power, let alone beat him.

Holyfield's heart of a warrior, the experts pontificated, would force him to pay the price for those tough fights, which left him only 4-3 in his last seven bouts. It was clear, the common wisdom went, that he was a shop-worn 34-year-old with no punch, legs or stamina left.
But Holyfield set a stiff price for Tyson, who couldn't ante up.

The former self-described "baddest man on the planet" who had promised to hurt Holyfield, paid through the nose, eyes and body, as Holyfield constantly beat Tyson to the punch, knocked him down in the sixth round, cut him, nearly knocked him out in the 10th round, and finally slammed him into submission in the 11th round.

Holyfield also knew when to clinch to rest up for his next assault and to get in out of the storm of Tyson's frustration, which because of his vaunted power always had a strong element of danger. In fact, the two fighters were warned in the third round by referee Mitch Halpern for holding.

Halpern finally stopped the fight at 37 seconds of the 11th round after Holyfield hit Tyson with nine unanswered punches, ending his onslaught with a big overhand right that sent Tyson reeling into the ropes.

From the opening bell, Holyfield signalled it was going to be an unusual fight for Tyson, who had easily won his first four fights since being released from prison last year. Holyfield came right at Tyson, hitting him first and forcing him to miss with big left hooks and overhand rights.

In the fourth round, Holyfield landed a very pretty combination of a right hand to the head and a left to Tyson's body. Shortly afterward Holyfield scored with a hard right uppercut, and Tyson came back with two left hooks to Holyfield's head.

Tyson had a good fifth round, wacking Holyfield with a left hook and a right to the side, followed by an uppercut that rocked Holyfield, who for most of the round would throw only two punches at a time before holding on.

But things turned sour for Tyson in the sixth round when a cut opened underneath his left eye, and with the sold-out crowd of 16,325 stamping its feet and chanting, "Holyfield, Holyfield, Holyfield," their hero dropped Tyson to the seat of his black satin trunks with a short left hand with only 36 seconds left in the round.
Tyson got up quickly and traded punches with Holyfield. But then Holyfield tatooed Tyson with a left-right-left-right combination that sent him into the ropes.
In the seventh round Tyson seemed to be complaining to the referee that Holyfield was gouging the cut under his eye, and later the two butted heads, bringing another look of complaint from Tyson.

The end for Tyson nearly came in the 10th round when Holyfield was hitting him almost at will, and he appeared ready to be knocked out after a very hard right-left, followed by a machine-gun fast series of punches that sent him into the ropes.

Then, at the opening of the 11th round, Tyson stood in front of his corner, hands down at his side, looking dazed, childlike, as if waiting for the final beating. Holyfield unloaded on Tyson and the referee ended the slaughter that crowned a new champion.

Holyfield, now 33-3, said he would rest before considering whether he will fight again. But, after earning $11 million for the fight, it would seem difficult for him to turn down what likely would be a $30 million payday in a return match.
The 30-year-old Tyson (45-2), who earned $30 million Saturday, said he would fight again, because, "I get so much money to fight, man, how can I not continue to fight."
